title: Harlem in Disorder: A Spatial History of How Racial Violence Changed in 1935
abstract: The violence that spread across Harlem on the night of March 19, 1935 was the first large-scale racial disorder in the United States in more than a decade and the first occurrence in the nation's leading Black neighborhood. However, as many observers pointed out, the events were 'not a race riot' of the kind that had marked the decades after the Civil War. Racial violence took a new form in 1935. Through a granular analysis of those events and the mapping of their locations, Harlem in Disorder reveals that Harlem's residents participated in a complex new mix of violence that was a multifaceted challenge to white economic and political power.

awards: ACLS Open Access Book Prize & Arcadia Open Access Publishing Award finalist (2026) — Multimodal

Full narrative

Stephen Robertson’s Harlem in Disorder examines the violence that spread across Harlem on March 19, 1935, arguing that it should not be read simply through the older model of a post-Civil War “race riot.” Instead, the book uses granular historical analysis and mapping to show how racial violence took on a different spatial and social form in this moment. That framing gives the work clear relevance for scholarship and public conversations about racial inequality, urban space, and the changing dynamics of collective violence.

The strongest signal in the record is its substantive policy and civic relevance. By linking violence to place, neighborhood structure, and racialized urban experience, the book speaks to questions that matter well beyond one historical episode: how racial conflict is organized in cities, how public space becomes contested, and how historians can explain violence in ways that inform present-day debates about inequality and social justice. The recorded subject alignment with gender equality also suggests a broader interpretive reach into questions of social power and vulnerability, even though the book’s central focus is historical rather than policy-oriented in a narrow sense.

The dissemination record shows some encouraging signs of access. OpenAIRE identifies the book in an open repository instance, indicating that at least one version is available openly, which can support reading, teaching, and reuse. The book also appears in a library holdings context, suggesting discoverability for instructors and researchers. In addition, the work has been recognized in reader-facing channels, including a LibraryThing note that it was a finalist for the ACLS Open Access Book Prize and Arcadia Open Access Publishing Award in 2026, pointing to visibility among engaged readers and within open-access publishing recognition.

At the same time, the measurable scholarly uptake is still thin in the current record. OpenAlex reports no citations yet, and there is no event data or other public-discourse signal available in the archive used here. That does not diminish the book’s substantive contribution; it simply means the documented impact is still early. For now, Harlem in Disorder is best characterized as a book with a strong interpretive agenda, open-access reach, and clear relevance to the study of racial violence and urban history, with its longer-term scholarly influence still to be established.
